items.stem: The conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo linked to control of coltan, gold and tin mines is best described as…
items.answer: a resource conflict with internationalised and identity dimensions
items.markingKey: a resource conflict with internationalised and identity dimensions. Armed groups such as M23 and neighbouring states are involved in a war shaped by minerals and identity.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Interstate war has disappeared since the end of the Cold War." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interstate wars still occur: Eritrea–Ethiopia (1998–2000), Russia–Georgia (2008), Armenia–Azerbaijan (2020) and Russia–Ukraine (2022–).
items.markingKey: Interstate wars still occur: Eritrea–Ethiopia (1998–2000), Russia–Georgia (2008), Armenia–Azerbaijan (2020) and Russia–Ukraine (2022–). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the classification of a conflict can itself be contested.
items.answer: Labels carry political consequences: calling a conflict “terrorism” delegitimises a group, calling it a “civil war” may justify neutrality, and calling it “genocide” triggers legal obligations under the 1948 Convention.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Labels carry political consequences: calling a conflict “terrorism” delegitimises a group, calling it a “civil war” may justify neutrality, and calling it “genocide” triggers legal obligations under the 1948 Convention. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source D
In 2023 there were 59 state-based armed conflicts, the highest number recorded since 1946. Most were fought within states, but a growing share were internationalised, with external states contributing troops to one side.
— Uppsala Conflict Data Program, Organized Violence report (2024) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain why the trend described makes conflicts harder to end. [3]
items.answer: Internationalised intrastate conflicts involve more actors with their own interests, external supplies of weapons and money, and veto players who can block agreements, so the number of parties that must agree to peace increases and conflicts last longer.
items.markingKey: Internationalised intrastate conflicts involve more actors with their own interests, external supplies of weapons and money, and veto players who can block agreements, so the number of parties that must agree to peace increases and conflicts last longer. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Using the war in Sudan since April 2023 as an example, explain an intrastate conflict with internationalised dimensions.
items.answer: Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced over 10 million people, with atrocities reported in Darfur. A struggle between two armed factions of the state has drawn in external backers and created the world’s largest displacement crisis.
items.markingKey: Context (Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced over 10 million people, with atrocities reported in Darfur.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A struggle between two armed factions of the state has drawn in external backers and created the world’s largest displacement crisis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to an intrastate conflict with internationalised dimensions.

items.stem: A student claims: "Ethnic conflicts are caused by ancient hatreds between groups." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Constructivist and instrumentalist research shows that ethnic identity is often mobilised by elites for political ends; groups that coexisted for long periods (e.g. in Bosnia) were polarised by leaders and propaganda.
items.markingKey: Constructivist and instrumentalist research shows that ethnic identity is often mobilised by elites for political ends; groups that coexisted for long periods (e.g. in Bosnia) were polarised by leaders and propaganda. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: To what extent are identity-based conflicts more difficult to resolve than resource conflicts? [15]
items.answer: Identity conflicts are often harder to resolve because claims seem indivisible, but most conflicts combine both dimensions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: identity claims are indivisible (Jerusalem, Kashmir); resources can be shared (wealth-sharing in Sudan’s 2005 CPA); most conflicts mix identity and resources (DRC); elite mobilisation can be reversed. Possible judgement: Identity conflicts are often harder to resolve because claims seem indivisible, but most conflicts combine both dimensions. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Kaldor’s concept of “new wars” no longer explains contemporary conflict."
items.answer: The concept still captures many intrastate conflicts, but the return of interstate war shows that “old” war has not disappeared.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the Russia–Ukraine war is a conventional interstate war with trench warfare and artillery; state armies remain central in Sudan, Gaza and Myanmar; critics (Kalyvas) argue “new” features existed in older civil wars. items.stem: Briefly explain why asymmetric conflicts are difficult for stronger states to win.
items.answer: Insurgents avoid conventional battle, blend into civilian populations and aim to outlast the stronger side’s political will; heavy-handed responses can increase local support for insurgents, as in Afghanistan (2001–2021).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Insurgents avoid conventional battle, blend into civilian populations and aim to outlast the stronger side’s political will; heavy-handed responses can increase local support for insurgents, as in Afghanistan (2001–2021). items.stem: Explain the difference between intrastate conflict and interstate conflict.
items.answer: Interstate conflict is fought between states, usually by regular armed forces; intrastate conflict takes place within a state, involving government forces and non-state armed groups or groups fighting each other.
items.markingKey: Interstate conflict is fought between states, usually by regular armed forces; intrastate conflict takes place within a state, involving government forces and non-state armed groups or groups fighting each other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict (1988–2023) and explain what it reveals about an identity-based territorial conflict.
items.answer: Armenia and Azerbaijan fought over the Armenian-populated enclave; Azerbaijan’s offensive of September 2023 led to the exodus of over 100,000 Armenians. Competing national claims to territory and identity drove a conflict that combined interstate war with ethnic displacement.
items.markingKey: Context (Armenia and Azerbaijan fought over the Armenian-populated enclave; Azerbaijan’s offensive of September 2023 led to the exodus of over 100,000 Armenians.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Competing national claims to territory and identity drove a conflict that combined interstate war with ethnic displacement. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to an identity-based territorial conflict.

items.stem: Which term describes diamonds mined in war zones and sold to finance armed groups, as in Sierra Leone in the 1990s?
items.answer: Conflict (blood) diamonds
items.markingKey: B. The Kimberley Process (2003) was set up to stop the trade.

items.stem: Distinguish between the security dilemma and deliberate aggression.
items.answer: In a security dilemma conflict arises from mutual fear and misperception of defensive actions; in deliberate aggression an actor intends to expand or attack regardless of others’ behaviour.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why grievances are more likely to lead to violence when groups are excluded from power.
items.answer: Excluded groups lack peaceful channels to address injustice; horizontal inequalities combined with political exclusion (Stewart; Cederman, Gleditsch and Buhaug) give leaders both a motive and a mobilising narrative for rebellion. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Collier’s greed theory means that rebels are simply criminals." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Collier’s point concerns the feasibility of rebellion: economic opportunity explains where rebellion can be sustained, not necessarily individual motives; later work stressed that greed and grievance interact.
items.markingKey: Collier’s point concerns the feasibility of rebellion: economic opportunity explains where rebellion can be sustained, not necessarily individual motives; later work stressed that greed and grievance interact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source D
The factors that explain civil war are not those that create grievances, but those that make rebellion feasible. Where rebellion is financially and militarily possible, it will occur; the motives of rebels are less important than the opportunities available to them.
— Paul Collier, Anke Hoeffler and Dominic Rohner, “Beyond Greed and Grievance: Feasibility and Civil War”, Oxford Economic Papers (2009) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain how the source challenges explanations of conflict based on injustice. [4]
items.answer: It argues that grievances are common but do not explain where war occurs; what matters is opportunity – funding, weak states, recruits – so injustice-based explanations miss the conditions that make rebellion possible.
items.markingKey: It argues that grievances are common but do not explain where war occurs; what matters is opportunity – funding, weak states, recruits – so injustice-based explanations miss the conditions that make rebellion possible. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "grievance".
items.answer: In conflict theory, a sense of injustice arising from inequality, political exclusion, repression or discrimination that motivates rebellion
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: in conflict theory, a sense of injustice arising from inequality, political exclusion, repression or discrimination that motivates rebellion. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Syrian uprising and civil war (2011– ) shows the interaction of grievance and identity in conflict.
items.answer: Protests against Assad’s regime after drought, unemployment and repression turned into civil war with sectarian dimensions and foreign intervention. Political repression and economic grievances triggered revolt, while sectarian mobilisation and external actors transformed it into a prolonged war.
items.markingKey: Context (Protests against Assad’s regime after drought, unemployment and repression turned into civil war with sectarian dimensions and foreign intervention.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Examine the view that the security dilemma is the main cause of interstate conflict. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: The security dilemma explains escalation between wary states, but revisionist intentions and domestic politics often matter more.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: arms races and fear before 1914; NATO enlargement and Russian threat perception (Mearsheimer’s argument on Ukraine); pre-emptive logic in South Asia. Arguments against: deliberate revisionist aims (Russia’s denial of Ukrainian statehood); nationalism and domestic politics; resource and territorial disputes. Possible judgement: The security dilemma explains escalation between wary states, but revisionist intentions and domestic politics often matter more. items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the multiplication of parties makes conflicts harder to resolve.
items.answer: More parties mean more potential spoilers, divergent interests and veto players; armed groups fragment and splinter, so agreements with one faction may not bind others, as in Libya or the DRC. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between UCDP conflict data and the Global Peace Index.
items.answer: The GPI is a composite index ranking how peaceful countries are, including militarisation and safety; UCDP records specific events and deaths of organised violence, providing conflict-level data rather than a country ranking.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "A high Global Peace Index ranking means a country has positive peace." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The GPI mainly measures the absence of violence and fear of violence (negative peace); positive peace is measured separately by the IEP’s Positive Peace Index.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Global Peace Index 2024 and explain what it reveals about the use of indices to identify trends.
items.answer: The GPI reported 56 active conflicts, the most since the Second World War, and a deterioration in peacefulness in 97 countries. Composite indicators allow trends to be compared, highlighting a global decline in peacefulness.
items.markingKey: Context (The GPI reported 56 active conflicts, the most since the Second World War, and a deterioration in peacefulness in 97 countries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Composite indicators allow trends to be compared, highlighting a global decline in peacefulness. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of indices to identify trends.

items.stem:
Source B
In 2023 there were 59 state-based armed conflicts, the highest number recorded since 1946. Most were fought within states, but a growing share were internationalised, with external states contributing troops to one side.
— Uppsala Conflict Data Program, Organized Violence report (2024) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source B about types of conflict. [3]
items.answer: 59 state-based conflicts in 2023; the highest number since 1946; most were intrastate but a growing share were internationalised
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: 59 state-based conflicts in 2023; the highest number since 1946; most were intrastate but a growing share were internationalised. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source D
The factors that explain civil war are not those that create grievances, but those that make rebellion feasible. Where rebellion is financially and militarily possible, it will occur; the motives of rebels are less important than the opportunities available to them.
— Paul Collier, Anke Hoeffler and Dominic Rohner, “Beyond Greed and Grievance: Feasibility and Civil War”, Oxford Economic Papers (2009) (paraphrased)

Identify three claims made in Source D about the causes of civil war. [3]
items.answer: civil war is explained by feasibility, not grievance; rebellion occurs where it is financially and militarily possible; rebels’ motives matter less than opportunities
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: civil war is explained by feasibility, not grievance; rebellion occurs where it is financially and militarily possible; rebels’ motives matter less than opportunities. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source B
Representatives of the Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) have rejected the terrorist label applied to them by some governments. They present the movement as defending Yemen against foreign military intervention and blockade, and argue that it is described as a rebel group mainly because it lacks international recognition.
— Summary of the Houthi movement’s publicly stated position, c. 2015–2016 (paraphrased in neutral terms)

With reference to Source B, explain how the source shows that the labelling of parties to conflict is contested. [4]
items.answer: The movement rejects “terrorist” and “rebel” labels and frames itself as a legitimate defender; this shows that labels reflect political power and recognition (statehood, UN membership) as much as behaviour.
items.markingKey: The movement rejects “terrorist” and “rebel” labels and frames itself as a legitimate defender; this shows that labels reflect political power and recognition (statehood, UN membership) as much as behaviour. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source D
Counting the dead is never a neutral exercise. Which deaths count, who counts them and how they are classified are political decisions that shape how the world responds to violence.
— Bear Braumoeller, political scientist, Only the Dead: The Persistence of War in the Modern Age (2019) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain why the measurement of conflict matters for international responses. [4]
items.answer: Classifications (e.g. war, genocide, terrorism) and counts influence media attention, aid, intervention and legal action; if deaths are undercounted or misclassified, responses may be inadequate or politicised.
items.markingKey: Classifications (e.g. war, genocide, terrorism) and counts influence media attention, aid, intervention and legal action; if deaths are undercounted or misclassified, responses may be inadequate or politicised. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source A
The new wars involve a blurring of the distinctions between war, organised crime and large-scale violations of human rights. Their goals are about identity politics, their methods involve the displacement of populations, and they are financed through a globalised war economy.
— Mary Kaldor, New and Old Wars: Organised Violence in a Global Era (1999; 3rd edition 2012) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source A, explain how the source suggests contemporary conflicts differ from interstate war. [4]
items.answer: Interstate wars were fought by states for geopolitical aims through battles between armies; the source describes conflicts pursuing identity aims, targeting populations through displacement and financed by criminal globalised economies, so war and crime overlap and civilians are the main victims.
items.markingKey: Interstate wars were fought by states for geopolitical aims through battles between armies; the source describes conflicts pursuing identity aims, targeting populations through displacement and financed by criminal globalised economies, so war and crime overlap and civilians are the main victims. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Greed is a more convincing explanation of civil war than grievance."
items.answer: Greed explains how wars are sustained, but grievance usually explains why they begin; the two are complementary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: statistical association with primary commodity dependence (Collier–Hoeffler); diamond-financed wars in Sierra Leone and Liberia; grievances are widespread but rebellion rare. Arguments against: horizontal inequalities and exclusion predict conflict (Stewart; Cederman); Syria 2011 began with grievances against repression; greed and grievance interact; resources often sustain rather than cause war. Supported judgement: Greed explains how wars are sustained, but grievance usually explains why they begin; the two are complementary. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Non-state actors are now more important than states in shaping armed conflict."
items.answer: Non-state actors have grown in importance, but states remain the decisive sponsors and adversaries in most conflicts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ISIS, the RSF and the Houthis control territory and populations; PMSCs extend conflicts (Wagner); most conflicts are intrastate. Arguments against: states remain the main suppliers of weapons and money; interstate war in Ukraine; state recognition and UN membership still determine legitimacy. Supported judgement: Non-state actors have grown in importance, but states remain the decisive sponsors and adversaries in most conflicts. items.stem:
Source B
The Global Peace Index 2024 finds that there are currently 56 conflicts, the most since the Second World War. They have become more international, with 92 countries involved in conflicts outside their borders. Peacefulness deteriorated in 97 countries.
— Institute for Economics and Peace, Global Peace Index 2024 (paraphrased)

With reference to Source B, explain why the data in the source might be used to argue that the international system is becoming less peaceful. [4]
items.answer: The rising number of conflicts, their increasing internationalisation and widespread deterioration in peacefulness suggest weakening restraints on violence and growing great-power and regional competition.
items.markingKey: The rising number of conflicts, their increasing internationalisation and widespread deterioration in peacefulness suggest weakening restraints on violence and growing great-power and regional competition. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Which scholar developed the concept of “new wars” in New and Old Wars (1999)?
items.answer: Mary Kaldor
items.markingKey: C. Kaldor contrasted new wars with Clausewitzian interstate wars.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "In Collier and Hoeffler’s model, the economic opportunity for rebellion, such as lootable natural resources, diaspora funding and low recruitment costs"?
items.answer: greed
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of greed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An irregular armed force, often local or ethnic, which may be allied with or tolerated by a government, such as the Janjaweed in Darfur"?
items.answer: militia
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of militia.

items.stem: Distinguish between UCDP conflict data and the Global Peace Index.
items.answer: The GPI is a composite index ranking how peaceful countries are, including militarisation and safety; UCDP records specific events and deaths of organised violence, providing conflict-level data rather than a country ranking.
items.markingKey: The GPI is a composite index ranking how peaceful countries are, including militarisation and safety; UCDP records specific events and deaths of organised violence, providing conflict-level data rather than a country ranking. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Interstate war has disappeared since the end of the Cold War." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Interstate wars still occur: Eritrea–Ethiopia (1998–2000), Russia–Georgia (2008), Armenia–Azerbaijan (2020) and Russia–Ukraine (2022–).
items.markingKey: Interstate wars still occur: Eritrea–Ethiopia (1998–2000), Russia–Georgia (2008), Armenia–Azerbaijan (2020) and Russia–Ukraine (2022–). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Collier’s greed theory means that rebels are simply criminals." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Collier’s point concerns the feasibility of rebellion: economic opportunity explains where rebellion can be sustained, not necessarily individual motives; later work stressed that greed and grievance interact.
items.markingKey: Collier’s point concerns the feasibility of rebellion: economic opportunity explains where rebellion can be sustained, not necessarily individual motives; later work stressed that greed and grievance interact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "States are always the most powerful actors in contemporary conflicts." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Non-state groups such as ISIS (which controlled territory with millions of people in 2014–17) or the RSF in Sudan can rival or exceed the power of state forces in parts of a country.
items.markingKey: Non-state groups such as ISIS (which controlled territory with millions of people in 2014–17) or the RSF in Sudan can rival or exceed the power of state forces in parts of a country. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A high Global Peace Index ranking means a country has positive peace." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The GPI mainly measures the absence of violence and fear of violence (negative peace); positive peace is measured separately by the IEP’s Positive Peace Index.
items.markingKey: The GPI mainly measures the absence of violence and fear of violence (negative peace); positive peace is measured separately by the IEP’s Positive Peace Index. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between intrastate conflict and interstate conflict.
items.answer: Interstate conflict is fought between states, usually by regular armed forces; intrastate conflict takes place within a state, involving government forces and non-state armed groups or groups fighting each other.
items.markingKey: Interstate conflict is fought between states, usually by regular armed forces; intrastate conflict takes place within a state, involving government forces and non-state armed groups or groups fighting each other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Poverty alone causes conflict." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many poor countries are peaceful; poverty raises risk mainly through weak state capacity, low opportunity costs of fighting and group inequalities combined with exclusion.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Kaldor’s concept of “new wars” no longer explains contemporary conflict."
items.answer: The concept still captures many intrastate conflicts, but the return of interstate war shows that “old” war has not disappeared.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the Russia–Ukraine war is a conventional interstate war with trench warfare and artillery; state armies remain central in Sudan, Gaza and Myanmar; critics (Kalyvas) argue “new” features existed in older civil wars. Arguments against: identity politics and war economies still drive conflicts in the DRC and the Sahel; private military companies (Wagner) and criminal finance blur war and crime; civilians remain the main victims. Supported judgement: The concept still captures many intrastate conflicts, but the return of interstate war shows that “old” war has not disappeared.

items.stem: "The security dilemma is the main cause of interstate conflict." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: The security dilemma explains escalation between wary states, but revisionist intentions and domestic politics often matter more.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: arms races and fear before 1914; NATO enlargement and Russian threat perception (Mearsheimer’s argument on Ukraine); pre-emptive logic in South Asia. Arguments against: deliberate revisionist aims (Russia’s denial of Ukrainian statehood); nationalism and domestic politics; resource and territorial disputes. Possible judgement: The security dilemma explains escalation between wary states, but revisionist intentions and domestic politics often matter more. items.answer: PMSCs create serious accountability problems that soft-law instruments have not solved.

items.stem: "Quantitative indices such as the Global Peace Index are of limited use to policymakers." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Indices are useful for trends and comparison, but must be combined with qualitative, local analysis.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: indicators and weights are value-laden; data gaps in conflict zones (Tigray); rankings hide local variation. Arguments against: allow comparisons over time and between countries; identify early warnings of deterioration; inform aid allocation and investment. Possible judgement: Indices are useful for trends and comparison, but must be combined with qualitative, local analysis.
